text: Once you know what the filesystem looks like, the next step is moving around it from the shell, without ever opening a graphical file manager. This lesson covers the handful of commands you'll type more than any others on the job: ls, cd, pwd, cp, mv, rm, mkdir, touch, cat, less, grep, and find.

pwd prints exactly where you are in the tree. ls -la lists the current directory, with -l giving permissions, owner, and size, and -a including hidden dotfiles. cd changes directory — cd dot-dot moves up one level, and cd with nothing takes you straight home.

mkdir creates a directory, and touch creates an empty file or just updates its timestamp without changing its contents. cp source destination copies a file, and mv does both moving and renaming — Linux treats them as the same operation. rm deletes a file, and rm dash r deletes a directory and everything inside it recursively. There's no recycle bin on Linux, so rm is permanent.

cat dumps a whole file straight to the terminal, which is fine for something short but useless for a multi-thousand-line log. less opens a file one screen at a time, lets you search forward with a slash, and quits with q — the right tool for anything longer than a screenful.

grep searches inside a file's content for a matching pattern, with -i for case-insensitive and -r to search an entire directory tree recursively. find searches the filesystem itself for files matching criteria, like a name pattern or how recently they were modified. grep answers what's inside a file; find answers which files exist.

Put those twelve commands together and you can navigate, inspect, search, and manage almost anything on a Linux box, over SSH, with nothing but a keyboard. Next up: users, groups, and the permission model that decides who's even allowed to run these exact commands against a given file in the first place.
